/MONDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Issued at 330 PM MDT Sat Oct 10 2026

The exceptionally warm weather pattern for this time of year will 
finally break down this week, as the weather will actually feel like 
October by the middle of the week. One more day of unusual warmth is 
anticipated for Monday. While the sprawling upper level low will 
remain to our west, the subtle short-wave providing forcing for the 
earlier shower activity will lift to our northeast. Synoptic descent 
will push in behind along with a drier airmass dropping precipitable 
water closer to seasonal averages. While some shower activity driven 
by SSW upslope flow will likely persist in Carbon County, expect a 
lull in the shower chances for much of the area Monday morning. High 
temperatures will still be around 10F above seasonal averages. We 
will still have enough moisture lingering to support high-based 
showers in the late afternoon and evening, but appreciable rainfall 
is unlikely. 

The warm pattern will finally break on Tuesday, with nearly all 
ensemble members in agreement. A northern branch shortwave trough 
passing well to our north apart from the stalled upper level low to 
our west will support a modest surface high pressure center over the 
northern Plains. This feature will push a cool front through the 
area Monday night, leading to a cooler day Tuesday. The frontal 
boundary is expected to stall against the Laramie range once again. 
So, while areas along and east of I-25 should be a good 10F or even 
15F cooler than Monday, Laramie and Rawlins may only drop a few 
degrees. As the front pushes in overnight, models are more 
consistently showing isentropic lift on the east side of the 
approaching upper level low developing over much of the area. Thus, 
expect to see shower coverage increasing Monday night into early 
Tuesday morning. Still, rainfall rates and amounts look light during 
this window. Look for another lull during the daytime hours on 
Tuesday as the forcing weakens temporarily. A few showers will 
probably linger across the area, but with much more limited 
coverage. Models are in good agreement now showing very strong 
isentropic lift and positive theta-e advection kicking up again 
Tuesday evening and lasting into Wednesday. This looks like the best 
window for beneficial rainfall for most of our area due to the more 
potent forcing. Snow levels will start around 10 kft and drop to 
8500 or even 8000 ft into Wednesday morning. Thus, snow is likely in 
the Snowy and Sierra Madre, and possible as low as the I-80 summit 
and Arlington/Elk Mountain areas. However, relatively few ensembles 
(10% or so) have the temperatures cold enough to support snow levels 
dropping to populated areas of southeast Wyoming, at least during 
the Tuesday night to Thursday morning period. 

Ensemble agreement falls apart completely Wednesday night and 
beyond. Models have diverged into two distinct camps with starkly 
different outcomes for our area. The primary piece of the puzzle 
driving this uncertainty is the track of a powerful and cold upper 
level low dropping out of Canada mid to late week. In one camp, the 
western ridge recovers quickly enough to deflect this trough to the 
east, pushing it into the Great Lakes area. In this case, the upper 
level closed low would get abandoned underneath the re-amplifying 
ridge, keeping unsettled weather but generally light winds and 
warmer temperatures, in place over our area. In the other scenario, 
the upper level low plunges into the US much further west, possibly 
as far as down the eastern front of the Rockies. This would first 
allow the the closed low to eject off to the northeast, and then 
bring a potent surge of cold air to the area on Friday. In this 
scenario, there would be potential for high winds across the plains 
on Thursday, followed by widespread freezing temperatures Friday. 
About 20% of total ensemble members push the trough far enough west 
to bring another round of upslope precipitation to the area, which 
would have much lower snow levels (likely snow down to at least 5000 
ft, if this scenario were to play out). Ensembles are split nearly 
exactly 50/50 right now, so there is not much insight into which is 
favored at this time. The official forecast straddles the middle 
between them at this time. 

While this week will provide improved chances for beneficial 
precipitation for much of the area, exact amounts are still quite 
uncertain. While ensemble means are fairly high, it is worth 
mentioning that there are a small number (10 to 15%) of extreme high 
end outlier scenarios that might be skewing the average. Ensemble 
median QPF generally ranges around 0.5 to 0.75" in southeast 
Wyoming, and 0.3 to 0.6" in western Nebraska. The NBM distribution
